clue.text: Turned up toes maybe spilling water

definitions.meaning: to turn up one's toes is a jokey idiom for dying
literally knocking over a pail with your foot sends its water everywhere

explanation.surface: Someone stubs a toe and knocks over a pail of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' flags that the literal reading is just one way the phrase could be taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are slang for dying, idiomatic expressions with the same meaning.

clue.text: Pupils embracing religious instruction, a work of 21 14

indicators.note: the group of pupils wraps its arms round the next piece, holding it inside

parts.note: a class is a group of pupils
RI is the school abbreviation for religious instruction

explanation.surface: A class taking scripture lessons studies a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 14 is the linked answer at 21-down and 14-across, the eighteenth-century novelist whose epistolary novel of this name is famously long.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a vast epistolary novel by that eighteenth-century writer, published 1748.

clue.text: Glider scotched, not killed, by 12

parts.note: a gliding creature that, in the Scottish play at 12, the king says has been wounded but not destroyed

explanation.surface: An aircraft is grounded but not wrecked by a Scottish monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Shakespeare's play at 12: 'We have scotch'd the snake, not kill'd it.' 'Glider' suggests an aircraft but means a slithering reptile; 'scotched' means wounded.
explanation.definitionFit: A legless reptile moves by gliding along the ground, and Shakespeare's tyrant uses it as his image of an injured threat.

clue.text: Not quite when I am for love, on second thoughts, for David

parts.note: a postscript, PS, is the note added at the foot of a letter after reflection

indicators.note: the letter I takes the place of the round letter that stands for love, a zero score in tennis

parts.note: not quite means almost

explanation.surface: A lover hesitates, rethinks, and decides on someone called David.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, as in tennis scores; 'when I am for love' swaps an I in for that O in ALMOST, giving ALMIST.
explanation.definitionFit: King David is traditionally credited with writing many of the Psalms, so he is the classic writer of sacred songs.

clue.text: Affection for anger?

definitions.meaning: heated feeling in an argument, as when someone speaks with heat

explanation.surface: A question about whether fondness can be swapped for fury.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word covers kindly feeling and the heat of temper, as in 'he replied with some heat'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both cordiality and heated passion, so it covers tenderness and temper alike.

clue.text: Moviemaker needs accountant and compère to get things straight

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant
a compère is an MC, master of ceremonies
to order things is to put them straight

explanation.surface: A film producer hires an accountant and a host to tidy up the business.
explanation.definitionFit: A portable video camera is a device for making home movies.

clue.text: See 19
18 unknown to slut coming in before novelist

indicators.note: the run of pieces enters the word for before, splitting it

parts.note: ante is Latin for before, as in ante-room
18-down's answer is abbreviated HON, as in an honorary secretary
Y is an algebraic unknown
trollop is an old word for a promiscuous woman

explanation.surface: An unpaid stranger and a loose woman make an entrance ahead of a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 points to 18-down, whose usual abbreviation is HON; 'to' joins it to TROLLOP before the lot goes inside ANTE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian writer of the Barsetshire series was a prolific novelist.

clue.text: Caspian, say, gets Annie's lad off

indicators.note: the letters are gone off, spoiled and out of order, so they need rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Annie gets rid of her boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'Annie's' is part of the fodder here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caspian is a vast landlocked body of salt water, the classic example of this kind.

clue.text: Deck trouble with sailors

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble
RN is the Royal Navy, hence sailors

explanation.surface: Sailors having bother on the ship's deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' looks like part of a ship but is a verb meaning decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck is to decorate, as in decking the halls.

clue.text: Kings entertaining painter turn left to get fur from sheep

indicators.note: the two kings play host to the painter, holding him between them

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king, so two kings give KK
ARA is an Associate of the Royal Academy, a painter
U as in a U-turn

explanation.surface: Royal hosts give an artist a reason to change direction and fetch a sheepskin.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an Asian breed of sheep whose curly lamb's fleece is prized as a pelt.

clue.text: Scottish king, an American subject, retaining award

indicators.note: the school subject keeps the award held within it

parts.note: Americans call mathematics math
CBE, Commander of the British Empire, is a British honour

explanation.surface: A US school subject wins a British honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour awarded by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The eleventh-century ruler of Scotland, made famous by Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: We come to it, getting up for a row

definitions.meaning: the burial service says we return to it in the end: ashes to ashes
add 'up' to the word and you have a fight or brawl

explanation.surface: An ominous statement about where we end up, then an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: the word plus UP makes a phrase meaning a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth's fine powder is where the funeral rite says our bodies end, and with 'up' added it means a scrap.

clue.text: See 21
Playing his cello, Highland leader appears on the Road to the Isles

definitions.text: on the Road to the Isles

indicators.note: the letters are played around with, like notes on an instrument
the leading letter of the word Highland is taken

explanation.surface: A Highland chief plays his cello while travelling the road westward to the Hebrides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Road to the Isles' is a Scottish song and the West Highland road from Fort William to Mallaig, which passes this loch at Glenfinnan.
explanation.definitionFit: A long freshwater lake in the western Highlands lies beside the route to the Hebrides celebrated in song.

clue.text: Man has a heavy defeat — listen to all he says

parts.note: he stands for a man
a rout is a crushing defeat

explanation.surface: A man is beaten badly and asks to be heard to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To let a person finish speaking without interruption is an idiomatic phrasal verb.

clue.text: Worry about woman in stream

indicators.note: the worry goes round the woman, enclosing her

parts.note: to fret is to worry
she refers to a woman

explanation.surface: Anxiety over a woman drowning in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fast stream, or a flood of fresh water from melting snow or rain.

clue.text: Nothing's for nothing, never mind about marriage

parts.note: free means costing nothing
love is a nil score in tennis

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that nothing is gained by marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing's' gives the tennis zero, with 's as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names relationships without the formality of wedlock.

clue.text: Getting nothing for being old and not being entertained

indicators.note: the second piece is hosted inside the first word

parts.note: hoary means grey with age, old
nor means and not

explanation.surface: An elderly person who is never invited out gets nothing for it.
explanation.definitionFit: An honorary post is unpaid, so its holder receives no salary.

clue.text: Box in wearing fewer clothes and drawers, a work of 8

indicators.note: the box sits in the word for less clothed

parts.note: barer means more naked
a chest is a box
those who draw or pull things are towers

explanation.surface: A box of underwear left by someone half-undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawers' seems to be underwear or a chest's parts, but means people who tow. 8 is 8-down.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1857 novel is the second of the Barsetshire chronicles by the Victorian author at 8.

clue.text: Concerned with Roman coin on the ground

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the as was a Roman copper coin

explanation.surface: Someone excited about an ancient coin lying on the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like soil, but is grounds, a basis for something.
explanation.definitionFit: Grounds for an action are its justification or cause.

clue.text: Strong man, hiding awfully cruel one and tough, was novelist

indicators.note: the strong man conceals the other pieces inside himself

parts.note: Samson is the biblical strong man

indicators.note: awfully signals the letters are treated terribly and jumbled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
hard means tough

explanation.surface: A strong man conceals a cruel streak and a hard heart, yet wrote novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' jumbles the letters of 'cruel' together with I into UELRIC; Samson is the biblical hero whose strength lay in his hair.
explanation.definitionFit: This eighteenth-century writer of long epistolary books is a key early English novelist.

clue.text: Take back part of the sound of silence

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is needed, a run inside its words

explanation.surface: A request to retract a piece of a song about silence.
explanation.definitionFit: To reverse or cancel an action is to retract it.

clue.text: Embarrass a party?

parts.note: a bash is a party

explanation.surface: A question of whether a party can be embarrassing.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone feel ashamed or awkward is to disconcert them.

clue.text: Talk food at naval base once

parts.note: chat means talk
ham is a kind of food

explanation.surface: Sailors talking about lunch at the old dockyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kent dockyard closed in 1984, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: This Kent town housed a Royal Navy dockyard for four centuries until 1984.

clue.text: Generous remarks that are defamatory about artist

indicators.note: the defamatory remarks go round the artist

parts.note: libel is defamation
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: Slanderous comments made about a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal means open-handed, giving freely.

clue.text: Unrestrainedly express feelings for quarter bit of 13

parts.note: E, east, is a compass quarter
a mote is a speck of dust, the answer at 13

explanation.surface: Someone gets emotional over a small speck.
explanation.definitionFit: To act out emotions theatrically is to overplay feeling.

clue.text: Listen to water falling from roof

definitions.meaning: the old sense of rainwater dripping from the edge of a roof

explanation.surface: A person hears rain dripping from the gutter.
explanation.walkthrough: The older noun meant the drip from a roof's edge; standing in it to overhear gave the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Snooping on a conversation is listening covertly, originally by standing under the dripping edge of a house.
